option_description: The host specification field in an NFS export policy entry that defines which clients are permitted to mount the share. Can be a wildcard ('*'), CIDR range ('192.168.1.0/24'), specific IP, or hostname. This is the primary access control gate for NFS mounts.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'unrestricted_nfs_export_policy' (score 8, high criticality) when export_host_pattern equals '*' or '0.0.0.0/0', or when those patterns are combined with 'no_root_squash'. A wildcard host allows any machine on any network segment to mount the share without authentication, enabling unauthorized data access and lateral movement. The regex check `^(\*|0\.0\.0\.0/0)$` confirms even equivalently formatted universal permits trigger the rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run exportfs with verbose flag on the NFS server to display all active export entries including their client host specifications.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines like '/data/shared  192.168.10.0/24(rw,sync,root_squash)' — the client field before the parenthesized options is the host pattern. A wildcard '*' indicates unrestricted access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the primary NFS exports configuration file directly to capture the host pattern field for each export line.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Two-column output of export path and client specification, e.g., '/backup *(rw,no_root_squash)'. The second column contains the host pattern.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On systems using exports.d drop-in directory, enumerate all export fragments to capture host patterns defined outside the main exports file.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Same two-column format as /etc/exports. Empty output means no drop-in export fragments exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use showmount to query exports as a remote client would see them, confirming what host patterns are effectively exposed on the network.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export list showing paths and allowed clients, e.g., '/data *' confirms world-accessible export.

option_description: The comma-separated list of mount options applied to each NFS export entry, controlling permissions (rw/ro), privilege mapping (root_squash, no_root_squash, all_squash), synchronization behavior (sync/async), and security flavor (sec=krb5p). These options collectively define the security posture of each individual export.
security_impact: The Rego policy 'unrestricted_nfs_export_policy' (score 8) has an aggravated condition that fires when a wildcard host pattern is combined with 'no_root_squash' in export_options, as this grants remote root users unfettered root-level access to the share. The 'nfs_root_squash_disabled' rule (score 8) also inspects this list indirectly through the root_squash_enabled and all_squash_enabled booleans derived from these options. Presence of 'no_root_squash' is the highest-risk single option, while 'rw' combined with weak host scoping amplifies exposure significantly.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use exportfs in verbose mode to display the full option set for each export entry as the kernel currently applies them.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output like '/data 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync,no_root_squash,no_subtree_check)' — extract the parenthesized portion as the options list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse /etc/exports directly to extract all options per export entry, including options that may not yet be active if the exports daemon has not been reloaded.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Per-export option strings like '/mnt/backup rw,async,no_root_squash'. Missing root_squash or all_squash in the options string indicates privilege escalation risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for no_root_squash specifically across all exports in a single targeted scan to quickly identify high-risk entries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing 'no_root_squash' with their file and line number. Any match requires immediate review. Zero output is the desired result.

option_description: A boolean indicating whether the NFS export applies root_squash, which maps any incoming request from UID 0 (root) on the client to the anonymous user (typically nobody/nfsnobody) on the server. When enabled, remote root users cannot exercise root privileges over files on the mounted share.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'nfs_root_squash_disabled' (score 8, high criticality) fires when both root_squash_enabled and all_squash_enabled are false. Without root_squash, a remote user who has or gains root on any authorized client can read, modify, or delete any file on the NFS share regardless of file ownership — effectively gaining root access to all shared data. The 'missing_or_weak_authentication_mechanism' rule also consults root_squash_enabled alongside export_client_scope when evaluating the overall authentication posture of the export.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check exportfs output for presence of root_squash in export options. Its absence or the explicit presence of no_root_squash means root_squash_enabled is false.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing option state per export. 'root_squash' present = true. 'no_root_squash' present or neither squash option present = false (NFS default is root_squash on modern distros, but verify explicitly).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse /etc/exports to determine the root_squash state per export entry, checking for explicit settings.
how_to_obtain.command: awk 'NF && !/^#/ {if ($0 ~ /no_root_squash/) print $1, "root_squash_enabled: FALSE"; else if ($0 ~ /root_squash/ || $0 ~ /all_squash/) print $1, "root_squash_enabled: TRUE"; else print $1, "root_squash_enabled: CHECK_DEFAULT"}' /etc/exports
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Per-export assessment. 'CHECK_DEFAULT' entries require verification of the NFS daemon default configuration, as the kernel default behavior may differ between distributions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the effective NFS server default settings from the nfsd configuration to understand whether root_squash is applied by default when not explicitly specified.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries controlling default squash behavior. If absent, refer to distro documentation — modern RHEL/Debian default to root_squash but this must be confirmed.

option_description: A boolean indicating whether the NFS export applies all_squash, which maps all remote user requests — including root — to the anonymous user on the server. This is more restrictive than root_squash alone, as it prevents any client-side user from retaining their UID/GID on the server, enforcing uniform anonymous access.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'nfs_root_squash_disabled' (score 8, high criticality) fires when both root_squash_enabled AND all_squash_enabled are false. all_squash provides an alternative safeguard: even if root_squash is absent, all_squash prevents any user (not just root) from carrying elevated privileges onto the server. However, all_squash should be combined with appropriate anonuid/anongid settings to avoid granting the anonymous user unintended access. When both squash options are disabled, the server fully trusts client-supplied UIDs, enabling trivial impersonation of any user.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan exportfs output specifically for all_squash option presence across all active exports.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count greater than 0 indicates at least one export has all_squash. Follow up with 'exportfs -v | grep all_squash' to identify which specific exports have it enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search /etc/exports and any drop-in configuration files for all_squash directives.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing 'all_squash' with file and line number. Zero output means no exports have all_squash configured. Cross-reference with root_squash_enabled status to determine if nfs_root_squash_disabled will fire.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Display a combined squash status summary for all exports to evaluate the combined root_squash and all_squash posture at once.
how_to_obtain.command: exportfs -v | awk '{printf "%-40s ", $1; if ($0 ~ /all_squash/) print "all_squash=YES"; else if ($0 ~ /no_root_squash/) print "all_squash=NO root_squash=NO [RISK]"; else if ($0 ~ /root_squash/) print "all_squash=NO root_squash=YES"; else print "all_squash=NO root_squash=DEFAULT"}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Per-export squash status table. Any '[RISK]' label indicates the nfs_root_squash_disabled rule will trigger.

option_description: A boolean indicating whether the NFS or SMB service requires cryptographic encryption of all data in transit. For NFS, this means NFSv4 with Kerberos using 'sec=krb5p' (which provides both authentication and payload encryption). For SMB, this means SMB encryption ('smb encrypt = required' in Samba or EncryptData=True in Windows). When false, all file data, metadata, and credentials traverse the network in cleartext.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'unencrypted_data_in_transit' (score 8, high criticality) fires when transport_encryption_enabled is false, and also fires for legacy protocol versions (nfsv2, nfsv3, smbv1) which cannot support encryption. Additionally, 'smb_signing_disabled' (score 5) interacts with this attribute — the smb_signing_required attribute is evaluated alongside transport encryption for SMB. Cleartext NFS or SMB traffic can be intercepted with standard packet capture tools (tcpdump, Wireshark) by any attacker with network access, exposing all file contents and potentially authentication credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NFS: check the sec= option in /etc/exports to determine if krb5p (encrypted) is required. For Samba: inspect smb.conf for smb encrypt setting.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NFS: 'sec=krb5p' = encrypted (true). 'sec=krb5' or 'sec=krb5i' = authenticated but not fully encrypted. 'sec=sys' or absent = cleartext (false). Samba: 'smb encrypt = required' = true; 'desired' or 'off' = false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows SMB servers, query the SMB server configuration via PowerShell to determine the EncryptData setting.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: EncryptData: True = transport_encryption_enabled is true. EncryptData: False = false. RejectUnencryptedAccess: True confirms enforcement is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture NFS traffic on the wire with tcpdump to confirm whether file data is visible in plaintext, validating the effective encryption state regardless of configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Readable file content or directory names in the strings output confirms cleartext transmission (false). Encrypted traffic produces only binary noise with no readable strings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NFSv4 Kerberos, verify the GSSAPI/Kerberos security flavor is negotiated by checking the mounted share's security flavor from a client.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'sec=krb5p' in mount options confirms encryption is active. 'sec=sys' confirms cleartext auth and no encryption.

option_description: A boolean indicating whether the SMB server mandates cryptographic message signing on all SMB connections. When required, every SMB message is signed with a keyed HMAC, ensuring message integrity and preventing tampering. When merely 'enabled' but not 'required', clients that do not support signing can still connect unsigned, leaving those sessions vulnerable.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'smb_signing_disabled' (score 5, medium criticality) fires when smb_signing_required is false AND smb_signing_enabled is false, or when signing is enabled but not required (allowing unsigned sessions). The 'unencrypted_data_in_transit' rule (score 8) also references smb_signing in its SMB protocol conditions. Without mandatory signing, attackers can perform NTLM relay attacks where captured authentication tokens are relayed to the storage server to mount shares under a legitimate user's identity, or perform man-in-the-middle attacks to modify SMB traffic in transit, injecting malicious file content or commands.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows Server, query the SMB server configuration via PowerShell to check both RequireSecuritySignature and EnableSecuritySignature.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RequireSecuritySignature: True = smb_signing_required is true. RequireSecuritySignature: False = false, even if EnableSecuritySignature is True (signing negotiated but not enforced).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Samba servers, inspect smb.conf for the server signing directive in the [global] section.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'server signing = mandatory' = smb_signing_required is true. 'server signing = auto' or 'server signing = disabled' = false. Absent setting defaults to auto (not mandatory) on most Samba versions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use smbclient to test whether the server accepts unsigned connections by attempting to negotiate without signing.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful share listing despite '--option=client signing=no' indicates signing is not required (false). 'NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED' or signing negotiation failure indicates mandatory signing is enforced (true).

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows Server, navigate to the Local Security Policy or Group Policy to verify the 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)' setting.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Open 'Local Security Policy' (secpol.msc) → Local Policies → Security Options → 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)'. Enabled = smb_signing_required is true.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy status shows 'Enabled' for mandatory signing (true) or 'Disabled' (false).

option_description: Controls whether the SMB server has message signing enabled at all. When enabled, the server advertises signing capability to clients, though connections from clients that do not request signing may still be accepted without it unless signing is also required.
security_impact: The Rego policy smb_signing_disabled fires in two conditions: when both smb_signing_required and smb_signing_enabled are false (signing completely absent), AND when smb_signing_required is false even if smb_signing_enabled is true. This means enabling signing without requiring it still triggers the finding, because unsigned relay-capable connections remain possible. The unencrypted_data_in_transit rule also considers signing status for SMB protocol versions. Without signing enabled, NTLM relay attacks allow attackers to impersonate legitimate storage clients and access shares.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows Server, use PowerShell to query the SMB server configuration and check whether security signature is enabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: EnableSecuritySignature: True indicates signing is enabled; RequireSecuritySignature: True indicates it is enforced. Both False means signing is completely disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Samba servers, inspect the smb.conf global section for the 'server signing' directive. Valid values are 'disabled', 'auto', 'mandatory'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'server signing = auto' means enabled but not required; 'server signing = mandatory' means required; absence of the directive defaults to auto on most Samba versions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Samba, use testparm to display the effective configuration including signing defaults that may not appear explicitly in smb.conf.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output will show the resolved 'server signing' value. If no line appears, the default applies (auto on Samba 4.x).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap with SMB scripts to probe the server's signing negotiation behaviour from a client perspective, confirming what the server actually advertises.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output includes 'message_signing: disabled', 'supported' (enabled but not required), or 'required'. 'disabled' or 'supported' indicates the smb_signing_disabled finding will trigger.

typical_values: false (Windows Server default for non-domain-controller roles)
true with RequireSecuritySignature also true on domain controllers
auto via Samba default (enabled but not required)

option_description: Identifies the specific file sharing protocol and version actively in use on the server. This covers both NFS variants (v2, v3, v4, v4 with Kerberos) and SMB variants (v1, v2, v3), representing the lowest active version when multiple are enabled simultaneously.
security_impact: The Rego unencrypted_data_in_transit rule unconditionally fires for nfsv2, nfsv3, and smbv1 because these protocol versions have no built-in encryption capability at all. For smbv2 and smbv3, the rule fires when smb_signing_enabled is also false, since those versions support signing but do not enforce it. NFSv4 with Kerberos (nfsv4_kerberos) is the only NFS variant that provides cryptographic authentication and optional encryption, making protocol version a primary determinant of multiple exposure rules.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows Server, check which SMB protocol versions are currently enabled using PowerShell.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: EnableSMB1Protocol: False and EnableSMB2Protocol: True is the baseline hardened state. Both True indicates SMBv1 is still active and should be recorded as 'smbv1'. SMBv3 is part of the SMB2 implementation in Windows; check dialect negotiation logs for v3 confirmation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux NFS servers, query rpcinfo to identify which NFS versions are registered and listening.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each line shows program number 100003 with version numbers (2, 3, 4). Presence of version 2 or 3 entries indicates legacy protocol versions are active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux NFS servers, check the NFS server configuration file for explicit version restrictions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries like 'vers3=n' or '--no-nfs-version 2,3' confirm older versions are disabled. Absence of explicit version pins means all supported versions (including v2/v3) are active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Samba, check the configured minimum and maximum SMB protocol versions in smb.conf.
how_to_obtain.command: testparm -s 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(min protocol|max protocol|server min protocol|server max protocol)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'min protocol = SMB2' or higher is expected. 'min protocol = NT1' (SMBv1) or absence of a min protocol setting means SMBv1 is active and should be recorded as 'smbv1'.

typical_values: nfsv3 (most common Linux NFS default, legacy environments)
smbv3 (Windows Server 2012 R2+ with dialect negotiation)
smbv1 (legacy Windows or unpatched Samba, should be absent)

option_description: Specifies the authentication mechanism negotiated for NFS export access, controlling how the server verifies client identity. Options range from no authentication ('none') through host-based UID/GID trust ('auth_sys') to cryptographically strong Kerberos variants ('krb5', 'krb5i', 'krb5p') that add authentication-only, integrity, and full privacy respectively.
security_impact: The Rego missing_or_weak_authentication_mechanism rule fires unconditionally when nfs_auth_flavor is 'auth_sys' or 'none', because both rely on client-asserted UID/GID values with no cryptographic verification. Any client that spoofs a UID can impersonate any user. The rule also fires when the flavor is not a Kerberos variant AND kerberos_configured is false, covering cases where a non-standard or misconfigured auth is in use. The unrestricted_nfs_export_policy rule references nfs_auth_flavor context to evaluate combined risk of wildcard exports plus weak auth.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/exports for the 'sec=' option on each export line. Multiple security flavors can be listed colon-separated.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: sec=krb5p is the most secure option. sec=sys or absence of sec= (defaults to auth_sys) is the common weak configuration. sec=none allows unauthenticated access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nfsstat or cat /proc/fs/nfsd/versions to verify running NFS server state, then use rpcinfo to confirm RPCSEC_GSS (Kerberos) registration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of rpcsec_gss (program 100303) in rpcinfo output confirms Kerberos/GSSAPI is operational. Absence means only AUTH_SYS is available regardless of exports configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS server, use showmount to display active exports and their options, then cross-reference with exports file for sec= settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lists exported paths and their allowed client patterns. Does not directly show sec= flags, but confirms which exports are active. Combine with grep on /etc/exports for complete picture.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a connected NFS client, use nfsstat to observe the security flavor of active mounts to confirm what is actually negotiated in practice.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'sec=krb5p' in the mount options confirms Kerberos with privacy. 'sec=sys' confirms AUTH_SYS is in use for that mount.

typical_values: auth_sys (default and most common in enterprise Linux deployments)
krb5i (Kerberos with integrity, common in hardened environments)
krb5p (Kerberos with full encryption, highest security)
none (occasionally seen on internal data-migration or legacy exports)

option_description: Indicates whether the NFS server host has the necessary Kerberos infrastructure in place to support Kerberos-based NFS authentication, including a valid keytab file containing an nfs/ service principal, a running GSSAPI proxy daemon (rpc-gssd or gssproxy), and a reachable KDC referenced in krb5.conf.
security_impact: The Rego missing_or_weak_authentication_mechanism rule fires when nfs_auth_flavor is not a Kerberos variant AND kerberos_configured is false. This means even if an administrator has set sec=krb5 in /etc/exports, if the Kerberos infrastructure is not actually operational, clients may fall back to or negotiate weaker auth. Confirming kerberos_configured=true is a prerequisite for trusting that Kerberos auth flavors are genuinely enforced and not silently downgraded.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the system keytab file for the presence of an NFS service principal, which is required for the server to authenticate via Kerberos.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output like 'nfs/server.example.com@EXAMPLE.COM' confirms a valid NFS service principal is present. Empty output or 'No such file' means Kerberos is not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that the GSSAPI daemon (rpc-gssd or gssproxy) is running, as it is required to process Kerberos credential exchanges for NFS.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl is-active rpc-gssd gssproxy 2>/dev/null; ps aux | grep -E '(gssd|gssproxy)' | grep -v grep
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'active' status for rpc-gssd or gssproxy, or a process listing for either daemon, confirms the GSSAPI infrastructure is running. Both inactive means Kerberos NFS is non-functional.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/krb5.conf to confirm it references a valid KDC for the expected realm, which is required for ticket validation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line like 'kdc = kdc.example.com' within a realm block confirms KDC is configured. An empty realms section or missing file means Kerberos is not configured for this host.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform an end-to-end kinit test using the NFS service keytab to confirm the KDC is reachable and the principal is valid.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful kinit followed by klist showing a valid ticket for the NFS principal confirms end-to-end Kerberos functionality. Errors like 'KDC unreachable' or 'principal unknown' indicate false configuration.

typical_values: false (most common; Kerberos NFS is rarely deployed outside enterprise or academic environments)
true (found in Active Directory-integrated Linux NFS servers and Hadoop/HPC clusters)

option_description: Enumerates all security principals (users, groups, or well-known SIDs) that have been granted Change or Full Control permission on the SMB share-level ACL, representing all identities capable of writing, modifying, or deleting files on the share.
security_impact: The Rego overly_permissive_smb_share_permissions rule fires when specific broad principals appear in write_principals: 'Everyone', 'Authenticated Users', 'Domain Users', or 'BUILTIN\Users'. These groups effectively encompass all domain or local users, meaning any authenticated identity (including compromised accounts) can write to the share. This is distinct from NTFS filesystem-level permissions; share-level ACLs provide the outer permission boundary and granting write to broad groups here defeats any tighter NTFS restrictions in practice.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows Server, use PowerShell to retrieve the share-level ACL for all shares or a specific share, showing principals and their access rights.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-SmbShareAccess -Name '<sharename>' | Select-Object Name, AccountName, AccessControlType, AccessRight | Format-Table -AutoSize
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each row shows a principal (AccountName) and their AccessRight (Read, Change, or Full). Extract all rows where AccessRight is 'Change' into write_principals.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the legacy net share command to enumerate all shares and their permissions in environments where PowerShell remoting is unavailable.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output includes a Permissions section listing principals. Note that 'net share' output is less structured than Get-SmbShareAccess and may truncate long ACLs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Windows Server Manager or Computer Management, navigate to shared folders to view and audit share permissions graphically.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Server Manager > File and Storage Services > Shares > right-click share > Properties > Permissions tab. Alternatively: Computer Management (compmgmt.msc) > Shared Folders > Shares > right-click > Properties > Share Permissions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The Share Permissions tab lists principals with Allow/Deny and permission level (Read, Change, Full Control). Screenshot or enumerate all entries where Change or Full Control is set to Allow.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query share ACLs remotely using PowerShell CIM for batch assessment of multiple servers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns only the Change and Full Control entries, providing a clean list for write_principals population.

typical_values: ['Everyone'] (highly permissive default on some legacy shares)
['Authenticated Users'] (common on departmental shares, overly broad)

option_description: Enumerates all security principals granted Full Control permission at the SMB share ACL level, meaning they can read, write, delete files, and also modify share permissions themselves. This is a superset of write access and represents the highest privilege tier on the share.
security_impact: The Rego overly_permissive_smb_share_permissions rule fires when 'Everyone', 'Authenticated Users', 'Domain Users', or 'BUILTIN\Users' appear in full_control_principals. Full Control at the share level includes the ability to change the share ACL itself, enabling privilege escalation where a compromised account in one of these broad groups could grant further access. In ransomware scenarios, Full Control for broad groups enables encryption of all share contents and deletion of shadow copies without any ACL barrier.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows Server, use PowerShell to retrieve only Full Control entries from the share ACL, which is the target population for this attribute.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lists only principals with Full Control. An empty result means no principal has Full Control at the share level (permissions may still exist at NTFS level). Presence of Everyone or broad groups is a critical finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For bulk assessment across all shares on a server, enumerate all shares and their Full Control principals in one pass.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-SmbShare | ForEach-Object { $share = $_.Name; Get-SmbShareAccess -Name $share | Where-Object { $_.AccessRight -eq 'Full' } | Select-Object @{N='Share';E={$share}}, AccountName }
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of all shares with their Full Control principals. Any row showing 'Everyone', 'Authenticated Users', 'Domain Users', or 'BUILTIN\Users' represents a policy violation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review share permissions via Computer Management console to visually identify Full Control grants on individual shares.
how_to_obtain.navigation: compmgmt.msc > Shared Folders > Shares > right-click target share > Properties > Share Permissions tab. Look for 'Full Control' column checkboxes that are checked for broad groups.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Full Control checked for specific service accounts or Administrators only is expected. Full Control checked for Everyone or Authenticated Users is the overly permissive condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use icacls to check NTFS permissions on the share root path as a complement to share-level ACL review, since effective permissions are the intersection of both.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Shows NTFS ACL entries. A principal with (F) indicates full control at the filesystem level. This supplements share ACL data; both levels must be reviewed for complete picture.

typical_values: ['Authenticated Users'] (common in environments migrated from NT4 defaults)

option_description: Tracks the number of calendar days elapsed since the last security patch was applied to the OS and storage daemon (nfsd, samba, etc.) on the storage server. Acts as a freshness indicator for the patching lifecycle.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags the 'unpatched_storage_server_software' exposure when this value exceeds 90 days. Storage daemons running on stale OS bases accumulate publicly known vulnerabilities over time, including remote code execution and privilege escalation CVEs that attackers can exploit without authentication.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On RPM-based systems, query the package manager history to find the most recent security update and calculate elapsed days from today.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of packages with timestamps; compare the most recent date to today to compute elapsed days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Debian/Ubuntu systems, review apt history logs for the last security-related upgrade event.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries with timestamps showing the most recent package operations; identify the most recent security update date.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On systems using dnf, inspect the dnf history to identify the last update transaction and its date.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of dnf transactions with dates; the most recent 'U' (update) transaction date is used to compute elapsed days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If a centralized patch management system (e.g., Red Hat Satellite, WSUS, Ansible Tower) is in use, query its dashboard or API for the last successful patch run date for this host.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Log into patch management console > select host by hostname/IP > view 'Last Patched' or 'Compliance Last Run' field.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A date field indicating the most recent completed patch application; convert to days elapsed.

option_description: An array of CVE identifiers representing publicly disclosed vulnerabilities that affect the currently installed storage daemon version and have not yet been remediated on this host.
security_impact: The Rego policy directly triggers the 'unpatched_storage_server_software' exposure whenever this array contains one or more entries. Any entry in this list represents a concrete, named vulnerability with public exploit potential, including critical Samba CVEs (e.g., CVEs in the EternalBlue class) or NFS daemon RCE bugs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use OpenSCAP to scan the host against the appropriate OVAL content for the installed OS and generate a vulnerability report.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of CVE IDs marked as 'true' (vulnerable) in the OVAL scan results, filtered to nfsd or samba packages.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Trivy to scan the host's installed packages directly and filter results to storage daemon packages.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of CVE IDs, severity ratings, and package names; collect all CVE IDs in the 'nfs' or 'samba' rows.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the NVD API for CVEs affecting the installed samba or nfs-utils version to identify unpatched vulnerabilities.
how_to_obtain.command: SAMBA_VER=$(samba --version | awk '{print $NF}'); curl -s "https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?keywordSearch=samba+${SAMBA_VER}&resultsPerPage=20" | python3 -m json.tool | grep cveId
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON response listing CVE IDs that match the installed samba version; filter to those with no available patch for this version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the vulnerability scan report for this host from your vulnerability management platform (Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7) and extract CVEs tied to nfsd or samba plugins.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Vulnerability scanner console > Assets > select host > Vulnerabilities > filter by plugin family 'NFS' or 'Samba' > export CVE column.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of CVE IDs with patch status 'unpatched' or 'open' for storage daemon plugins.

option_description: A boolean flag indicating whether the installed storage daemon (nfsd, samba, or equivalent) version has reached its end-of-life date and no longer receives security patch updates from the vendor.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'unpatched_storage_server_software' when this is true. An EOL daemon guarantees that newly discovered CVEs will never be patched, permanently locking the server into a vulnerable state. EOL Samba versions, for example, lack backported fixes for critical protocol-level vulnerabilities.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Determine the installed Samba version and cross-reference with Samba's official release lifecycle page.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output such as 'Version 4.14.5'; then check https://wiki.samba.org/index.php/Samba_Release_Planning to confirm if 4.14.x is still in support.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NFS on Linux, check the nfs-utils package version and cross-reference the distribution's EOL schedule.
how_to_obtain.command: rpm -q nfs-utils || dpkg -l nfs-kernel-server | grep nfs
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Package name and version string; verify against the OS vendor's security support timeline (e.g., RHEL 7 EOL June 2024).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the OS package manager to check if the installed distribution itself has entered EOL, which implies all its packages including nfsd are EOL.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/os-release; python3 -c "import distro; print(distro.name(), distro.version())" 2>/dev/null || lsb_release -a
how_to_obtain.expected_output: OS name and version; compare to the vendor's EOL calendar (e.g., Ubuntu 18.04 EOL April 2023).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Consult the vendor's official EOL/EOS matrix for the specific daemon version and record the support end date relative to today.
how_to_obtain.navigation: For Samba: https://wiki.samba.org/index.php/Samba_Release_Planning. For nfs-utils: check RHEL/Debian/Ubuntu support lifecycle pages. Compare installed version to listed end-of-maintenance dates.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A support end date that is either in the past (EOL = true) or in the future (EOL = false).

option_description: The network CIDR or IP address range that is permitted to reach storage service ports (NFS 2049, mountd/rpcbind 111, SMB 445, iSCSI 3260) as defined in firewall rules, cloud security groups, or network ACLs.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'network_exposure_without_firewall_restriction' when this value is '0.0.0.0/0' or '::/0' and exposed_storage_protocols is non-empty. An overly broad CIDR means any host on the internet or internal network can attempt to mount NFS shares or connect to SMB/iSCSI, dramatically increasing the attack surface.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the host-level firewall (iptables or nftables) for rules allowing inbound traffic to storage ports and extract the source CIDR.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -E '2049|445|111|3260'; nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | grep -E '2049|445|111|3260'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Firewall rules showing the source address field; '0.0.0.0/0' or 'anywhere' indicates unrestricted access. A specific subnet like '10.10.5.0/24' indicates restriction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-hosted storage servers, query the cloud provider CLI to retrieve security group ingress rules for the instance.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more CIDR strings. '0.0.0.0/0' confirms unrestricted internet access. A narrow subnet (e.g., '10.0.0.0/24') confirms restriction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the firewalld zone configuration files to identify which sources are allowed to reach storage-related services.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: XML entries with source IP or CIDR attributes; identify the broadest source CIDR present in rules permitting storage ports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host outside the intended client subnet, attempt a connection to port 2049 to verify whether the port is reachable from unauthorized segments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful connection ('open') from an unauthorized host confirms overly broad CIDR. 'Connection refused' or timeout from non-client hosts confirms restriction.

option_description: An array listing which storage protocol service ports (nfs, smb, iscsi, mountd) are reachable from network segments outside the designated client subnet, based on firewall and ACL analysis.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses a non-empty value for this attribute in combination with broad CIDRs to trigger 'network_exposure_without_firewall_restriction'. Each protocol in this list represents an active attack surface: exposed NFS enables unauthorized mounting, exposed SMB enables relay and brute-force attacks, exposed iSCSI enables block-level storage hijacking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap from a non-client network segment to scan all storage-related ports and identify which are reachable.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ports listed as 'open' in the nmap output that are reachable from the scanning host's non-client segment confirm exposure. Each open port maps to a protocol: 2049=nfs, 111=mountd, 445=smb, 3260=iscsi.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the storage server, list all listening sockets and identify which storage daemon ports are bound to all interfaces rather than specific addresses.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rows showing 'Local Address:Port'; '0.0.0.0:2049' or ':::2049' means all interfaces are listening and the protocol may be exposed depending on firewall rules.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review cloud security group rules for each storage port to enumerate which protocols have inbound rules permitting access from outside client subnets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON blocks for each permitted port; collect port numbers and map them to protocol names to populate the exposed list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall zone drop/reject rules to determine which storage ports lack a restricting deny rule for non-client subnets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACCEPT rules without source IP restrictions for storage ports confirm those protocols are exposed; map port numbers to protocol names.

option_description: A boolean indicating whether all firewall or security group rules permitting access to storage ports reference only specific, documented client subnets rather than broad any-source ranges like 0.0.0.0/0 or overly large supernets.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'network_exposure_without_firewall_restriction' immediately when this value is false, regardless of protocol exposure. This is the primary gating control: when false, any host reachable on the network can attempt to mount shares, brute-force SMB credentials, or connect to iSCSI targets, even if no known CVEs exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all iptables INPUT rules for storage ports and verify that every ACCEPT rule specifies a non-wildcard source address.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Source columns should show specific CIDRs (e.g., '10.10.5.0/24'). Any '0.0.0.0/0' entry means restriction is NOT enforced, set false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect firewalld rich rules or zone source entries to confirm storage services are bound to specific source subnets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rich rules should contain 'source address=X.X.X.X/YY' referencing only client subnets for NFS/SMB services. Absence of source scoping means restriction is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Azure-hosted storage, use the Azure CLI to retrieve NSG rules and confirm inbound rules for storage ports are source-restricted.
how_to_obtain.command: az network nsg rule list --nsg-name <nsg-name> --resource-group <rg> --query "[?destinationPortRange=='2049' || destinationPortRange=='445'].{Name:name,Source:sourceAddressPrefix}" --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Source column should show a specific CIDR, not '*' or 'Internet'. Any '*' source means subnet restriction is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review cloud console security group or firewall rule settings for the storage server instance to verify all inbound rules for storage ports list specific source CIDRs.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Instances > select instance > Security tab > Security Groups > Inbound rules > review Source column for ports 111, 445, 2049, 3260. Any '0.0.0.0/0' entry means false.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Every storage port rule has a specific subnet as source (e.g., '10.10.5.0/24'), not '0.0.0.0/0' or 'Anywhere'.

option_description: A boolean indicating whether NFS mount and unmount events are captured in a persistent log facility such as syslog or auditd, providing a record of which clients mounted which shares and when.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'inadequate_access_logging_and_auditing' when this is false. Without mount event logs, there is no record of unauthorized clients successfully mounting shares, making it impossible to detect exfiltration attempts or to conduct forensic investigation after a breach involving an NFS mount from a compromised host.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether rpc.mountd is configured with verbose logging flags and whether mount events appear in syslog.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Flags like '-l' or '--log-level=7' in mountd options indicate logging is enabled. Journal output should contain mount/unmount event lines. Absence of entries or no -l flag means logging is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check auditd rules for syscall-level mount event capture on exported paths.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Audit rules containing '-S mount -S umount2' confirm syscall-level mount logging. Empty output means no auditd-based mount logging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search existing syslog or journal for recent NFS mount events to confirm that events are actually being written.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'mounted|nfsd|mountd' /var/log/syslog /var/log/messages 2>/dev/null | tail -20; journalctl -u nfs-server --since '7 days ago' | grep -i mount
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log lines showing client IP addresses and mount paths confirm logging is active. Absence of any mount-related log entries within an active environment suggests logging is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the NFS server configuration for logging verbosity settings that enable mount event recording.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Variables like 'RPCMOUNTDOPTS="-l"' or '[mountd] debug=1' confirm mount logging is configured. Missing or empty logging flags mean it is not enabled.

option_description: A boolean indicating whether read, write, and delete operations performed on NFS-exported filesystem paths are recorded in an audit log via mechanisms such as auditd filesystem watches, kernel audit rules, or NFSv4 native audit support.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'inadequate_access_logging_and_auditing' when this is false. Without file access audit logging, an attacker who successfully mounts a share can read, modify, or delete files without any trace in logs. This also prevents compliance requirements (PCI-DSS, HIPAA) from being met for audit trails on sensitive data stores.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List active auditd watch rules for exported filesystem paths to confirm file access events are being captured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules like '-w /exports/data -p rwxa -k nfs-access' confirm file-level audit logging on exported paths. No '-w' rules for export paths means file access logging is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that auditd is running and that the audit log file contains recent file access events from NFS-exported paths.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl is-active auditd; ausearch -k nfs-access --start today 2>/dev/null | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: auditd status 'active' combined with ausearch results showing SYSCALL records for open/read/write/unlink on export paths confirms logging is working. No results means no file access audit rules are in effect.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the audit rules configuration directory for watch rules covering NFS export directories.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines like '-w /srv/nfs/backups -p rwxa -k file-access' confirm coverage of export paths. No matches mean exported directories are not under audit watch.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the audit log for recent file operation events on exported paths to confirm events are being written in practice, not just configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SYSCALL audit records with syscall names (open, read, write, unlink) and PATH records showing the actual file paths confirm active logging. Absence of records in a busy environment indicates logging is not functioning.

option_description: Controls whether failed authentication and authorization attempts on the NFS/SMB server are written to system logs, including denied mount requests, AUTH_NULL rejections, and Kerberos ticket failures.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags inadequate_access_logging_and_auditing when failed_auth_logging_enabled is false. Without this logging, brute-force mount attempts, UID spoofing under AUTH_SYS, and Kerberos misconfiguration failures go undetected, eliminating the ability to identify unauthorized access attempts or support forensic investigation after a breach.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search system logs for existing NFS denial or rejection messages to confirm whether failed auth events are currently being captured.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(denied|rejected|AUTH_NULL|krb5|permission denied)' /var/log/syslog /var/log/messages 2>/dev/null || journalctl -u nfs-server -u rpc.mountd --since '24 hours ago' | grep -iE 'denied|reject|auth'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing mount denial events or Kerberos failures if logging is active; empty output suggests logging is not enabled or no events have occurred.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/nfs.conf for the debug or verbosity settings that control NFS daemon logging granularity.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries such as 'debug=1' under [nfsd] or [mountd] sections indicate enhanced logging; absence of debug settings implies default minimal logging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the running rpc.mountd process arguments and rpcdebug bitmask to see if mount-level logging is active.
how_to_obtain.command: rpcdebug -m mountd -s 2>/dev/null; ps aux | grep -E 'mountd|nfsd' | grep -v grep
how_to_obtain.expected_output: rpcdebug output showing active debug flags (e.g., PROC, AUTH) confirms verbose failure logging; no flags indicates minimal logging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Samba/SMB deployments, review smb.conf for log level settings that capture authentication failures.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'log level = 2' or higher, with 'logging = syslog' or a defined log file path, confirms SMB auth failure logging is enabled.

typical_values: false (default — most Linux NFS deployments ship with minimal logging)
true (hardened or compliance-driven environments using rpcdebug flags or syslog configuration)

option_description: Controls whether changes to export policies, file permissions (chmod/chown), and ACLs on exported filesystem paths are captured in an audit log, typically via the Linux audit subsystem (auditd).
security_impact: The Rego policy flags inadequate_access_logging_and_auditing when permission_change_logging_enabled is false. Without auditing of permission changes, an attacker who has gained access can silently escalate privileges by modifying ACLs or export options, widen the export scope, or alter file ownership on sensitive paths—all without leaving a traceable record.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List active auditd rules to confirm whether watch rules exist for exported directories with write and attribute-change permissions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output such as '-w /export -p wa -k nfs_perm_change' confirms that write and attribute change events on exported paths are being audited.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review persistent auditd rule files for watch entries covering exported paths and permission-related syscalls.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules matching exported directory paths with '-p wa' or syscall rules for chmod/chown confirm permission change logging is persistently configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search the audit log for recent permission change events on exported paths to verify the rules are producing output.
how_to_obtain.command: ausearch -k nfs_perm_change --start today 2>/dev/null | head -40; ausearch -sc chmod --start today 2>/dev/null | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AVC or SYSCALL records for chmod/chown/setxattr operations on monitored paths confirm active logging; no output may indicate no changes occurred or rules are absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the auditd service is running and the audit daemon is not in backlog-overflow or silent-fail mode.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'active' for service status; 'enabled 1' and 'failure 1' or '2' in auditctl -s output confirms the audit subsystem is operational.

typical_values: false (default — auditd watches on NFS export paths are rarely preconfigured)
true (CIS-benchmarked or PCI-DSS-compliant systems with explicit auditd rules for exported directories)

option_description: Indicates whether the underlying storage volume hosting NFS/SMB export data has at-rest encryption enabled, such as dm-crypt/LUKS block device encryption, ZFS native dataset encryption, or equivalent hypervisor/cloud volume encryption.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags unencrypted_data_at_rest when volume_encryption_enabled is false. Without at-rest encryption, anyone with physical access to storage media, hypervisor console access, or snapshot-level access can read raw filesystem data without any network-layer authentication, bypassing all NFS/SMB access controls entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether block devices backing the export paths use LUKS encryption by inspecting dm-crypt mappings and LUKS headers.
how_to_obtain.command: lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT | grep -i crypt; cryptsetup luksDump $(df /export 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR==2{print $1}') 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(LUKS|Version|Cipher)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: LUKS header output with 'Version', 'Cipher name', and 'UUID' fields confirms dm-crypt/LUKS encryption is active on the backing device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For ZFS-backed storage, check the encryption property on the dataset hosting the export path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'encryption' column showing 'aes-256-gcm' or similar cipher with 'keystatus = available' confirms ZFS native encryption is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check /proc/mounts and device mapper tables to identify if exported paths are backed by encrypted devices.
how_to_obtain.command: dmsetup table 2>/dev/null | grep crypt; cat /proc/mounts | grep -E '(crypt|luks)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: dmsetup output showing 'crypt' target type for the device backing the export mount point confirms encryption is in use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-hosted volumes (AWS EBS, Azure Managed Disk, GCP Persistent Disk), query the cloud API to verify volume encryption status.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-volumes --query 'Volumes[*].[VolumeId,Encrypted,KmsKeyId]' --output table 2>/dev/null; az disk list --query '[*].{name:name,encrypted:encryptionSettingsCollection.enabled}' -o table 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Encrypted: true' and a KMS key ID in the output confirms cloud volume encryption is enabled.

typical_values: false (common in on-premises NAS/NFS deployments where disk encryption is not enabled by default)
true (cloud-hosted volumes with default encryption policies or explicitly LUKS-encrypted Linux storage servers)

option_description: Indicates whether the storage volume—which may lack at-rest encryption—is actively exported and reachable by remote clients over network protocols such as NFS or SMB, compounding physical-access risk with network-level exposure.
security_impact: The Rego policy includes a compounding condition in unencrypted_data_at_rest: when volume_encryption_enabled is false AND volume_accessible_over_network is true, an unencrypted volume is exposed to network attackers who need not have physical media access. This combination transforms a physical-access risk into a remote network exploitation risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all active NFS exports to determine if the volume's mount path is being served over the network.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export entries listing the volume path (e.g., '/data/storage') alongside client scope and options confirm NFS network accessibility.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check active SMB share definitions to determine if the volume is accessible via Samba.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Share definitions with the volume path listed under an active SMB share confirm SMB network accessibility.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan NFS and SMB ports from a remote host to confirm the volume's storage protocols are reachable over the network.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Open ports 2049 (NFS) or 445 (SMB) with service identification confirms the volume protocols are network-accessible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/exports directly to identify if the volume path appears in any export line, indicating it is configured for network sharing.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any non-commented line containing the volume path confirms it is configured as an NFS export.

typical_values: true (any NFS or SMB server by definition has volumes accessible over the network)
false (storage servers with network services disabled or volumes not yet exported)

option_description: Indicates whether the NFS export definition in /etc/exports scopes access to specific hostnames, IP addresses, or subnets ('host_restricted') or uses a wildcard/global pattern ('global') that permits any client to mount the share.
security_impact: The Rego policy world_readable_sensitive_exports fires when export_scope is 'global' combined with sensitive paths and weak auth. Additionally, unrestricted_nfs_export_policy fires directly on wildcard host patterns. A global scope means any host that can reach NFS port 2049 can attempt to mount the share, completely defeating network-layer access control and enabling reconnaissance or data exfiltration from any compromised host on the network.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/exports and supplemental drop-in export files for wildcard or global host specifications on each export line.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines where the client field is '*', '0.0.0.0/0', or a broad subnet like '192.168.0.0/8' indicate a global or overly permissive export scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use exportfs -v to display the currently active (kernel-loaded) export table including client scope for all exports.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output listing export paths with their client scope — entries showing '<world>' or '*' confirm global scope; specific IPs or hostnames confirm host_restricted scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the NFS server's published mount list from a remote or local client perspective using showmount to see what is visible network-wide.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Everyone' or '*' in the client column of showmount output confirms global/world export scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host NOT in the intended client list, attempt to query available exports to verify whether host restriction is enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If exports are visible from an unauthorized host, the scope is effectively global regardless of the configured client list.

typical_values: global (unfortunately common in internal NFS deployments where '*' is used for convenience)
host_restricted (best practice — specific IP, FQDN, or CIDR entries in /etc/exports)

option_description: The read/write permission applied to an NFS export entry, either 'ro' (read-only) or 'rw' (read-write), controlling whether mounting clients can modify data on the exported filesystem path.
security_impact: The Rego policy world_readable_sensitive_exports evaluates both 'ro' and 'rw' modes when combined with global scope, sensitive paths, and weak auth. An 'rw' export with global scope and weak authentication is particularly severe, enabling any client to delete, overwrite, or implant malicious content. Even 'ro' with global scope exposes sensitive data to any host that can reach the server, making it a world-readable share by definition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read /etc/exports and identify the access mode option (ro or rw) in the export options for each share definition.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'rw' confirms write access is granted; 'ro' confirms read-only access. Note that NFS defaults to 'ro' if no option is specified.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use exportfs -v to view the effective access mode currently loaded into the kernel for each active export.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each export entry shows its access mode in parentheses — e.g., '/backup  *(rw,sync,no_subtree_check)' confirms rw mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Samba/SMB exports, check the 'writable' or 'read only' directive in smb.conf for each share definition.
how_to_obtain.command: testparm -s 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(read only|writable|write ok)'; smbclient -L localhost -N 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'read only = No' or 'writable = Yes' confirms rw SMB access; 'read only = Yes' confirms ro mode.

typical_values: rw (common for operational shares; problematic when combined with global scope)
ro (appropriate for distribution shares, but still dangerous when globally scoped with sensitive paths)

option_description: Indicates whether any exported NFS/SMB path contains or is known to contain sensitive data categories, including backup archives, configuration files, credential stores, database dumps, or user home directories.
security_impact: The Rego policy world_readable_sensitive_exports only fires when exports_contain_sensitive_paths is true, making this a critical gating condition. Without this flag set, a globally-scoped rw export may appear lower risk. When true, combined with global scope and weak authentication, it indicates that sensitive data—potentially including credentials, backup archives, or regulated information—is accessible to any network client, representing a high-likelihood path to data breach or credential theft.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect export paths in /etc/exports against known sensitive path patterns including backup directories, home directories, and configuration paths.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any matching path (e.g., '/backup', '/home', '/etc') confirms the export contains a sensitive path category.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List the contents of exported directories to identify sensitive file types such as database dumps, password files, private keys, and archive files.
how_to_obtain.command: for path in $(exportfs -v 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u); do find "$path" -maxdepth 3 -name '*.sql' -o -name '*.dump' -o -name '*.tar.gz' -o -name 'shadow' -o -name '*.key' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name 'id_rsa' 2>/dev/null | head -5; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of .sql, .dump, .tar.gz, shadow, .key, .pem, or id_rsa files within exported paths confirms sensitive data is present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the storage administrator or data owner to determine the intended data type and sensitivity of each exported path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that exported paths contain backup data, configuration archives, home directories, or credential-related files classifies exports_contain_sensitive_paths as true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check SMB share paths defined in smb.conf for sensitive path patterns if SMB is in use alongside or instead of NFS.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SMB share path entries matching sensitive directory patterns confirm that SMB exports also contain sensitive data.

typical_values: true (extremely common — NFS is frequently used specifically to share backup and home directory data)
false (only for purpose-built public distribution shares, software repositories, or scratch storage with no sensitive data)

option_description: Controls the authentication flavor used for NFS exports, determining whether clients authenticate via standard UNIX UID/GID trust (sys/AUTH_SYS), Kerberos (krb5, krb5i, krb5p), or without any authentication (none). This governs how client identity is established before granting access to the share.
security_impact: The Rego policy 'world_readable_sensitive_exports' fires when auth_mechanism is 'none' or 'sys' AND the export is global with sensitive paths present. AUTH_SYS provides no cryptographic verification, meaning any client that spoofs a UID can impersonate any user. 'none' provides zero identity assurance. Only krb5, krb5i (with integrity), or krb5p (with privacy/encryption) provide cryptographic client identity guarantees that prevent impersonation attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/exports on the NFS server and look for the 'sec=' parameter within each export entry's options list.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export lines such as '/data 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sec=krb5p,root_squash)'; absence of sec= implies default of sys.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the running exportfs state to see active export options including security flavor as reported by the kernel.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing each exported path with options including sec=krb5p, sec=sys, or similar.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On an NFS client, use rpcinfo or nfsstat to interrogate the server's supported security flavors for a specific export.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Listed RPC programs and versions; mount options on client will show sec= flavor negotiated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the showmount command from a client to enumerate exports and then inspect the mount options negotiated for the security flavor.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exported directories listed; /proc/mounts shows sec=krb5p or sec=sys for mounted shares.

typical_values: krb5p (Kerberos with full encryption; most secure)

option_description: Describes how backup agent credentials or service account passwords are persisted within configuration files on the storage server. Values range from plaintext storage through hashed or encrypted representations to references that delegate secret retrieval to a dedicated secrets manager.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'insecure_backup_credential_storage' fires immediately when credential_storage_format equals 'plaintext', regardless of file permissions. A second condition fires when the format is not plaintext, secrets_manager_reference, or none BUT config_file_world_readable is true and secrets_manager_enforced is false—covering weakly protected hashed or encrypted credentials. Plaintext credentials harvested via local file read (possible after any lateral movement) grant direct access to backup infrastructure, enabling data exfiltration or destruction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect known backup agent configuration file locations for password fields and determine if values are human-readable strings, base64, hashes, or vault references.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: password=MyS3cret (plaintext), password={AES256}encryptedblob (encrypted), password=$vault:secret/backup/pass (secrets manager reference), or password=$6$salt$hash (hashed).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check .netrc files on the storage server which are commonly used by backup agents for FTP/SFTP credentials and often contain plaintext passwords.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries like 'machine backupserver login svcaccount password MyPlaintextPwd' indicate plaintext storage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search for backup daemon configuration files across common install paths and examine password-related fields to classify storage format.
how_to_obtain.command: find /etc /opt /var -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.ini' -o -name '*.cfg' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -lEi 'backup|bacula|veeam|commvault|netbackup|amanda' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -Ei 'password|passwd|secret' 2>/dev/null | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing credential fields; analyst must classify format (plaintext string vs hash pattern vs encrypted blob vs vault path).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview backup administrators and review backup agent deployment runbooks or configuration management templates (Ansible, Puppet, Chef) to determine the intended and actual credential storage method.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review Ansible playbooks/roles for backup agent configuration tasks; inspect vault_password_file or lookup('hashi_vault') usage patterns.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or code showing secrets_manager_reference (e.g., HashiCorp Vault lookup), encrypted vault files, or — as a finding — hardcoded plaintext variables.

typical_values: plaintext (common in legacy or ad-hoc deployments; high risk)
hashed (uncommon for passwords that must be presented to remote services)
secrets_manager_reference (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, CyberArk; best practice)
none (no credentials required; applicable to certificate-based auth scenarios)

option_description: Indicates whether backup agent or storage daemon configuration files containing credentials are accessible to non-owner, non-privileged OS users due to overly permissive file mode bits (e.g., 644, 640 with broad group, or 666). Even if credentials are not stored in plaintext, readable config files can expose encryption keys, vault tokens, or connection strings.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'insecure_backup_credential_storage' includes a condition that fires when config_file_world_readable is true AND credential_storage_format is not plaintext, secrets_manager_reference, or none AND secrets_manager_enforced is false. This captures the scenario where credentials are nominally protected (hashed or encrypted) but the protection is undermined by any local user being able to read the file and attempt offline attacks or steal vault tokens. This is particularly dangerous on multi-user storage servers or after a web application compromise grants local file read.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List permissions on all backup agent configuration files using stat to check for world-readable (other read bit set) or group-readable permissions with a broad group.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: -rw-r--r-- root root /etc/backup.conf indicates world-readable (true); -rw------- root root indicates not world-readable (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use find with permission filter to directly list any credential-containing config files that have read bits set for group or others.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any line where position 5 (group read) or position 8 (other read) is 'r' for a credential-containing file constitutes a world-readable finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Directly test specific known backup configuration file paths for world-readable permissions using a numeric mode check.
how_to_obtain.command: for f in /etc/backup.conf /etc/bacula/bacula-fd.conf /opt/NetBackup/bp.conf /etc/amanda/amanda.conf ~/.netrc; do [ -f "$f" ] && stat -c '%a %n' "$f"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mode values where last digit >= 4 (e.g., 644, 664, 666) indicate world-readable; 600 or 640 with appropriate group are acceptable.

typical_values: true (misconfigured: mode 644 or 666 commonly found in default package installs)

option_description: Reflects whether organisational policy backed by technical controls (configuration management enforcement, CI/CD pipeline checks, or runtime injection) mandates that backup agent credentials are retrieved dynamically from a dedicated secrets manager rather than stored statically in configuration files on the storage server. This is a policy and control maturity indicator rather than a single file setting.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'insecure_backup_credential_storage' uses secrets_manager_enforced as a mitigating factor: even when credential_storage_format is not ideal and config_file_world_readable is true, the rule's second condition only fires when secrets_manager_enforced is false. This recognises that a technical enforcement mechanism (e.g., Vault Agent sidecar injection, AWS IAM roles for EC2 that prevent static credentials) provides defence-in-depth. Without enforcement, static credentials inevitably drift into config files during operational shortcuts or emergency changes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review configuration management code (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, Terraform) for the storage server role to determine if secrets are injected from a vault rather than templated as static values.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of vault lookup calls (e.g., lookup('hashi_vault', 'secret/backup/password')) indicates enforcement; hardcoded variable assignments indicate non-enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for secrets manager agent processes (Vault Agent, AWS SSM Agent with Parameter Store) running on the storage server that would dynamically provide credentials.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep -E 'vault agent|ssm-agent|conjur|cyberark' | grep -v grep; systemctl list-units --state=active | grep -E 'vault|ssm|conjur'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active vault-agent or aws-ssm-agent processes indicate dynamic secret injection capability; absence combined with static config files indicates non-enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the backup agent configuration for Vault Agent template syntax or AWS Secrets Manager ARN references that indicate runtime secret retrieval.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ARN references or Vault template directives confirm secrets manager integration; no such references suggest static credential storage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organisation's backup agent onboarding runbook and security policy documents to determine if a formal requirement exists for secrets manager usage and whether it is technically enforced via pipeline gates.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review internal wiki/Confluence backup policy pages, CI/CD pipeline security scanning rules (e.g., Checkov, tfsec), and change management approval records for secrets manager requirements.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written policy mandate plus evidence of automated scanning that would reject plaintext credentials in IaC constitutes enforcement; policy without technical controls does not.

typical_values: false (most common; organisations have policy intent but lack technical enforcement)
true (mature organisations with HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or CyberArk enforced via IaC pipelines)

option_description: Indicates whether at least one active, automated, read-only snapshot schedule is configured on the shared storage volume. Snapshots create point-in-time copies of data that cannot be modified by clients mounting the share, providing a recovery mechanism that survives ransomware encryption events or accidental/malicious deletion.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'absence_of_snapshot_or_immutable_backup_protection' fires when both snapshot_policy_enabled and worm_policy_enabled are false (no protection at all), and also fires when snapshot_policy_enabled is true but worm_policy_enabled is false AND snapshot_retention_days is less than 7. This means enabling snapshots is necessary but not sufficient alone—they must be retained long enough to outlast ransomware dwell time. Without snapshots, any client with write access can permanently destroy all data on the share.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux with ZFS, list all snapshot schedules and existing snapshots for the storage pool hosting the NFS export.
how_to_obtain.command: zfs list -t snapshot | head -20; systemctl status zfs-auto-snapshot.* 2>/dev/null || crontab -l | grep snapshot; zfs get com.sun:auto-snapshot <dataset_name>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Snapshot entries like 'tank/data@zfs-auto-snap_daily-2024-01-15' and enabled cron jobs or systemd timers confirm snapshot_policy_enabled=true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For LVM-backed NFS exports on Linux, check for active LVM snapshot volumes and scheduled snapshot cron jobs.
how_to_obtain.command: lvs -o lv_name,lv_attr,origin | grep snapshot; crontab -l | grep -i snap; ls -la /etc/cron.*/snapshot* /etc/cron.d/*snap* 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: LV attributes showing 's' (snapshot) type and cron entries for snapshot creation scripts confirm active snapshot policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NetApp ONTAP storage systems, navigate to the volume snapshot policy configuration in System Manager to verify active snapshot schedules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NetApp System Manager > Storage > Volumes > [Select Volume] > Protection > Snapshot Copies > Snapshot Policy; verify a policy is assigned and enabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An assigned snapshot policy (e.g., 'default' or custom) with active schedules showing hourly/daily/weekly counts greater than zero confirms snapshot_policy_enabled=true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the NFS server's snapshot scheduler using vendor CLI tools (NetApp ONTAP CLI or Dell EMC PowerStore CLI) to enumerate volume snapshot policies.
how_to_obtain.command: volume snapshot policy show -vserver * 2>/dev/null || ssh admin@<filer> 'volume snapshot show' 2>/dev/null || pvesh get /nodes/<node>/storage 2>/dev/null | grep -i snapshot
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy entries with enabled=true and schedule counts confirm snapshot_policy_enabled=true; empty output or disabled policies indicate false.

typical_values: false (common in manually configured or cost-optimised environments; high risk)
true (standard in enterprise NAS platforms; NetApp default policies enabled out of box)

option_description: Indicates whether a WORM (Write Once Read Many) or immutable storage policy is active on the backup share, preventing any modification or deletion of stored objects or files within the defined retention period. Unlike snapshots which can sometimes be deleted by administrators, true WORM policies enforce immutability at the storage layer, resisting even privileged administrative deletion.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'absence_of_snapshot_or_immutable_backup_protection' fires when both snapshot_policy_enabled and worm_policy_enabled are false, and also fires when snapshots exist but retention is under 7 days and worm_policy_enabled is false. WORM provides a stronger guarantee than snapshots alone because snapshots may be deleted if an attacker gains admin credentials to the storage system. WORM enforced by hardware/firmware (NetApp SnapLock Compliance mode, S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode) cannot be overridden even by storage administrators, providing protection against insider threat and ransomware that achieves admin-level access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On NetApp ONTAP systems, check for SnapLock volumes and their compliance mode using the CLI.
how_to_obtain.command: ssh admin@<ontap_filer> 'volume show -fields snaplock-type,snaplock-expiry-time' 2>/dev/null || volume show -vserver * -fields snaplock-type 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: snaplock-type of 'compliance' or 'enterprise' confirms WORM policy; 'non-snaplock' or empty indicates worm_policy_enabled=false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux with ZFS, check for ZFS object immutability features or check if the share backend is on an immutable filesystem layer.
how_to_obtain.command: zfs get immutable <dataset> 2>/dev/null; chattr -R +i /path/to/backup/share 2>/dev/null && lsattr /path/to/backup/share | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files with 'i' attribute flag in lsattr output indicate immutability set; ZFS immutable property 'on' confirms WORM equivalent protection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For S3-backed NFS gateways (e.g., AWS Storage Gateway, MinIO), query the S3 Object Lock configuration on the underlying bucket via AWS CLI.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-object-lock-configuration --bucket <backup-bucket-name> 2>/dev/null; aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket <backup-bucket-name>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ObjectLockConfiguration with ObjectLockEnabled='Enabled' and Rule.DefaultRetention confirms WORM; empty response indicates not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NetApp ONTAP, navigate to System Manager to verify SnapLock compliance settings on the volume hosting the backup share.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NetApp System Manager > Storage > Volumes > [Select Volume] > Security > SnapLock; verify Type is 'Compliance' and minimum retention period is set.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SnapLock Type showing 'Compliance' with a retention period confirms worm_policy_enabled=true; 'Not configured' indicates false.

typical_values: false (default in most environments; WORM requires explicit licensing and configuration)
true (financial services, healthcare, and regulated industries using NetApp SnapLock, S3 Object Lock, or EMC DataDomain retention lock)

option_description: Specifies the number of days that point-in-time snapshots are retained before automatic purging. This value directly determines the recovery window available after a ransomware event, accidental deletion, or data corruption incident. A value of zero means snapshots are taken but immediately purged or no retention policy exists.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'absence_of_snapshot_or_immutable_backup_protection' includes a specific condition: when snapshot_policy_enabled is true but worm_policy_enabled is false AND snapshot_retention_days is less than 7, the exposure still fires. This reflects the operational reality that ransomware typically maintains a dwell time of days to weeks before triggering encryption, meaning a 1-3 day snapshot window is insufficient to recover from an attack that corrupted data before detection. The minimum threshold of 7 days represents a practical floor, and many frameworks recommend 30-90 days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On ZFS systems, query the auto-snapshot retention configuration for daily, weekly, and monthly snapshot schedules to determine the effective minimum retention window.
