how_to_obtain.command: zfs get com.sun:auto-snapshot:keep,com.sun:auto-snapshot:daily,com.sun:auto-snapshot:weekly <dataset> 2>/dev/null; zfs list -t snapshot -o name,creation -s creation | tail -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Property 'keep' values for each schedule (e.g., daily:7, weekly:4) and oldest snapshot creation date allow calculation of effective retention days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect cron-based snapshot management scripts or configuration files that define keep counts and schedule intervals for LVM or filesystem-level snapshots.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Variables like KEEP_DAILY=7 or retention_days=30 in scripts; combined with schedule frequency allows computation of retention_days (keep_count * schedule_interval_days).

how_to_obtain.instruction: On NetApp ONTAP, retrieve the snapshot policy schedule counts and map to retention days using the CLI.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Schedule entries showing daily count=7, weekly count=4 etc.; daily count directly equals minimum retention days for daily snapshots.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Calculate actual retention from existing snapshots by finding the oldest snapshot timestamp and computing the delta to today.
how_to_obtain.command: zfs list -t snapshot -o name,creation -s creation 2>/dev/null | head -5; lvs -o lv_name,lv_time --sort lv_time 2>/dev/null | grep snap | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Oldest snapshot creation date; current date minus oldest snapshot date equals effective retention_days. Values below 7 are flagged by policy.

typical_values: 0 (no retention policy; snapshots deleted immediately or feature disabled)
30 (common enterprise standard; meets most compliance framework requirements)
90 (financial services and healthcare standard; aligns with PCI DSS and HIPAA audit windows)

option_description: Specifies the OS user account under which the NFS (nfsd, rpc.mountd) or SMB (smbd, nmbd) daemon process executes. This determines the OS-level privilege context of the daemon, which dictates the blast radius if the daemon process is compromised through a vulnerability—whether the attacker gains root system access or is constrained to a limited service account.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'excessive_daemon_privileges' fires in three conditions, all centred on daemon_process_user equalling 'root': when the daemon runs as root alone; when it runs as root and no dedicated_service_account_exists; and when it runs as root with cap_net_bind_or_sys_admin capabilities. Running NFS or SMB daemons as root means that a successful exploit of daemon-level vulnerabilities (e.g., buffer overflows in nfsd or Samba RCE CVEs) results in immediate full system compromise rather than being contained to a low-privilege service account. This is particularly dangerous given Samba's historical CVE record (EternalBlue-class vulnerabilities, PrintNightmare variants).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect running NFS and SMB daemon processes and their effective user accounts using ps with user column display.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep -E 'nfsd|rpc\.mountd|rpc\.statd|rpc\.nfsd|smbd|nmbd|winbindd' | grep -v grep | awk '{print $1, $11}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output like 'root /usr/sbin/nfsd' indicates daemon_process_user=root (finding); 'nfsnobody /usr/sbin/rpc.nfsd' or 'nobody' indicates a service account.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect NFS daemon configuration files for user directives that override the default process user.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NFS_SERVER_USER=nfsnobody or User=nfsnobody confirms non-root service account; absence of directive or root value indicates running as root.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For systemd-managed NFS or Samba services, inspect the service unit file for the User= directive that controls process execution context.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl cat nfs-server smbd nmbd 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^User=|^Group='; systemctl show nfs-server smbd --property=User,Group 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: User=nfsnobody or User=smbservice indicates a dedicated service account; no User= line means the service runs as root by default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Samba, inspect smb.conf for security-related daemon user directives that affect process privilege level.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(security|server role|dedicated keytab file|become|root preexec|username map)' /etc/samba/smb.conf 2>/dev/null; testparm -s 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'security|server role'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Security mode and server role settings; combined with ps output confirms effective daemon user. smbd worker processes typically inherit from parent smbd user context.

typical_values: root (default for most Linux NFS server implementations; high risk)
nfsnobody (recommended dedicated NFS service account; UID 65534)
nobody (common fallback service account; shared with other services)
daemon (generic service account; less isolation than dedicated account)
nfsuser or smbservice (site-specific dedicated service accounts; best practice)

option_description: Controls whether the NFS or SMB daemon runs under a dedicated non-root, non-login service account rather than the root user or a generic system account. This isolates daemon privileges from the rest of the system.
security_impact: The Rego rule excessive_daemon_privileges fires when daemon_process_user is root and dedicated_service_account_exists is false. A daemon running as root means any vulnerability in nfsd or smbd grants immediate full system compromise. A dedicated account with a non-interactive shell limits blast radius to only what that account can access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check /etc/passwd for a service account with a non-interactive shell and UID >= 1000
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line such as 'nfs-server:1001:/usr/sbin/nologin' indicates a compliant dedicated account

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify which user account the running NFS or SMB daemon process belongs to
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Process user column should show a non-root dedicated service account name, not 'root'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the NFS or Samba configuration for an explicit User directive specifying the service account
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line like 'daemon user = nfs-server' or absence of root in user directives

option_description: Tracks whether the NFS or SMB daemon process has been granted elevated Linux capabilities such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE or CAP_SYS_ADMIN beyond the minimum required to function. These capabilities can be assigned via file capabilities or directly to the process.
security_impact: The Rego rule excessive_daemon_privileges fires when daemon_process_user is root and daemon_has_cap_net_bind_or_sys_admin is true simultaneously. CAP_SYS_ADMIN is nearly equivalent to full root access, enabling mount operations, namespace manipulation, and kernel module loading. Granting these to a storage daemon dramatically expands exploitation potential for any daemon-level vulnerability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the capability sets of the running NFS daemon process from /proc and decode them
how_to_obtain.command: cat /proc/$(pgrep -x nfsd || pgrep -x smbd | head -1)/status | grep -i cap && capsh --decode=$(cat /proc/$(pgrep -x nfsd || pgrep -x smbd | head -1)/status | grep CapEff | awk '{print $2}')
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show only minimal capabilities. Absence of cap_sys_admin and cap_net_bind_service in CapEff indicates compliant state

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for file-based capabilities assigned to the NFS or SMB daemon binary
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty output means no file capabilities are set. Any output containing cap_sys_admin or cap_net_bind_service should be flagged

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use getpcaps to list all capabilities for all NFS-related process IDs
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each PID should show either an empty capability set or only operationally justified capabilities without sys_admin or net_bind_service

option_description: Indicates whether the storage management interface, NAS web console, or backup agent is still authenticated with the factory-default username and password provided by the vendor in product documentation or firmware.
security_impact: The Rego rule default_or_shared_service_account_credentials fires immediately when uses_default_vendor_credentials is true, regardless of any other configuration. Default credentials are publicly listed in vendor manuals, CVE databases, and attacker toolkits, making them trivially exploitable for unauthorized management access, data exfiltration, or destructive operations against the storage system.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the NAS or storage management console using documented vendor default credentials (e.g., admin/admin, admin/password, or vendor-specific defaults from product documentation)
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to the storage appliance web UI (typically http or https on port 80, 443, or 8080). Attempt authentication with the vendor default username and password listed in the product quick-start guide or support portal.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful login with default credentials confirms the finding is true. Failed authentication suggests defaults have been changed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request evidence of initial credential change during provisioning by reviewing the change management ticket or build runbook for the storage system
how_to_obtain.navigation: Interview the storage administrator or review the system commissioning checklist. Ask whether vendor defaults were changed during initial setup and request the date of the credential change.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented credential change entry with a timestamp after initial provisioning indicates the finding is false

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review authentication audit logs for the management interface for evidence of login with the default account name
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of successful logins under the default vendor account name suggests credentials have been rotated

option_description: Identifies whether the same service account credentials, API key, or password are configured on more than one storage server, backup system, or NAS appliance. This creates a lateral movement path where compromising a single credential grants access to multiple systems.
security_impact: The Rego rule default_or_shared_service_account_credentials fires when service_account_shared_across_systems is true and credential_rotation_enforced is false. Shared credentials mean a credential harvested from one system (e.g., from a plaintext config file) immediately provides access to all systems sharing that credential, enabling mass storage compromise in a single step.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Compare backup agent or storage management configuration files across systems for identical username and password values
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each storage or backup system should reference a unique credential identifier or secrets manager path rather than a shared literal password

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the service account inventory from the identity and access management team and cross-reference which accounts are configured on multiple systems
how_to_obtain.navigation: Interview the storage or IAM administrator. Request a listing of all service accounts used across storage and backup systems and ask whether any accounts are intentionally shared across system boundaries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each storage system should have a uniquely named service account or API credential. Any account appearing on more than one system should be documented with a waiver or remediated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the secrets manager or credential vault to check if the same secret is referenced by multiple storage system entries
how_to_obtain.command: vault list secret/storage/ 2>/dev/null || aws secretsmanager list-secrets --query 'SecretList[?contains(Name,`storage`)]' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each entry should be uniquely named and scoped to a single system. Identical secret values across multiple entries indicate sharing.

option_description: Indicates whether an automated or procedural policy exists to periodically rotate credentials for storage management service accounts and backup agents, ensuring that compromised credentials have a limited usable lifetime.
security_impact: The Rego rule default_or_shared_service_account_credentials fires when service_account_shared_across_systems is true and credential_rotation_enforced is false together. Without rotation, a harvested credential remains valid indefinitely. Rotation limits the window of exploitation even when credential sharing cannot be immediately eliminated and reduces risk from credentials exposed in historical backups or log files.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's IAM or password management policy documents for defined rotation intervals for storage service accounts
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request the IAM policy document or privileged access management policy from the security or operations team. Verify whether storage service accounts are explicitly included in the scope with a defined maximum credential age.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented rotation policy with a specific interval (e.g., 90 days) that includes storage service accounts indicates the control is enforced

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the secrets manager for the last rotation date of storage-related credentials
how_to_obtain.command: aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id storage-backup-svc --query '{LastRotatedDate:LastRotatedDate,RotationEnabled:RotationEnabled}' 2>/dev/null || vault read -field=last_rotation_time secret/storage/backup-agent 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RotationEnabled should be true and LastRotatedDate should be within the policy-defined rotation interval from the current date

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check audit logs or the secrets manager rotation history for evidence of periodic credential changes
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing periodic credential change events at regular intervals confirm rotation is occurring

option_description: Controls whether the NFS server or shared storage volume enforces per-user or per-share disk usage limits, preventing any single user or client from exhausting the entire storage volume capacity.
security_impact: The Rego rule missing_disk_quota_enforcement fires when disk_quotas_enabled is false, and also fires when it is true but quota_scope is 'none'. Without quotas, a compromised client, a misconfigured backup job, or a denial-of-service attack can fill the storage volume entirely, causing all dependent systems including other backup targets to fail. Quotas provide a containment boundary for storage abuse.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether quota support is active on the filesystem by inspecting active mount options in /proc/mounts
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more lines containing usrquota, grpquota, or prjquota confirm quota mount options are active on the relevant filesystem

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run repquota to confirm the quota subsystem is active and reporting usage
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Tabular output showing user or group quota limits and usage per filesystem confirms quotas are enabled and enforced

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NAS appliances, check the share or volume quota settings in the management console
how_to_obtain.navigation: Log in to the NAS management web interface. Navigate to Storage > Volumes or Shares > Quota Settings. Verify that a quota policy is enabled and assigned to the target volume or share.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A quota policy showing hard and soft limits greater than zero assigned to the volume confirms disk_quotas_enabled is true

option_description: Defines the granularity at which storage quotas are applied on the NFS or shared storage volume. Options are per-user (individual UID limits), per-group (GID limits), per-share (export-level limits), combined (multiple quota types active), or none (no quotas enforced).
security_impact: The Rego rule missing_disk_quota_enforcement fires when disk_quotas_enabled is true but quota_scope is 'none', capturing the case where the quota subsystem is initialized but no actual limits are configured. Per-user quotas provide the strongest individual containment. Per-share quotas provide coarse aggregate limits. A scope of 'none' means quotas are nominally enabled but provide no real protection against storage exhaustion attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Determine which quota types are configured by inspecting mount options and running quota reporting tools

option_description: Enumerates all storage and management protocols currently active and listening on the storage server, including both operational protocols such as NFS and SMB and potentially insecure legacy protocols such as FTP, telnet, rsh, and unencrypted HTTP management interfaces.
security_impact: The Rego rule unused_protocols_and_services_enabled fires independently for each insecure protocol found in the list: ftp, telnet, rsh, and http each trigger the rule when insecure_legacy_protocols_justified is not true. Each enabled but unused protocol adds an attack surface with potentially unpatched code. Telnet and rsh transmit credentials in cleartext. FTP has known anonymous access risks. These protocols often receive less security attention than primary storage protocols.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all TCP and UDP ports currently listening to identify active storage and management protocol services
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each listening port maps to a protocol: 21=ftp, 23=telnet, 80=http, 111=portmapper/rpc, 139/445=smb, 2049=nfs, 3260=iscsi. Only operationally required protocols should appear.

option_description: Controls whether enabled insecure or legacy network protocols on the shared storage server (FTP, telnet, rsh, HTTP management interfaces) have formal documented business justification and compensating controls recorded in organizational security governance artifacts such as change management records, security exception registers, or configuration management documentation.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule 'unused_protocols_and_services_enabled' triggers a low-criticality exposure (score 2) whenever FTP, telnet, rsh, or HTTP appear in 'input.enabled_storage_protocols' AND 'input.insecure_legacy_protocols_justified' is false. These protocols transmit credentials and data in cleartext, lack modern authentication, and receive reduced patch attention, unnecessarily expanding the attack surface of the storage server. Setting this attribute to true suppresses the exposure finding only when a legitimate, approved exception with compensating controls (e.g., network isolation, protocol proxies, enhanced monitoring) is on record, ensuring the risk acceptance is deliberate and auditable rather than an oversight.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's security exception register or risk acceptance log to locate any approved exception covering the specific insecure protocols (FTP, telnet, rsh, HTTP management) enabled on the NFS/SMB storage server. Confirm the exception references the specific server hostname or IP, identifies the protocol(s), lists compensating controls, includes an expiry date, and bears an authorizing signature from the security or risk team.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Security GRC platform (e.g., ServiceNow GRC, Archer) → Risk Register or Exception Management → filter by asset name or IP of the storage server → review active exceptions for FTP/telnet/rsh/HTTP
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An approved, non-expired exception record explicitly naming the storage server and the insecure protocol(s), with documented compensating controls and an authorizing approver; absence of such a record means this attribute should be false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the storage server's service configuration files to confirm which legacy protocols are actually enabled, then cross-reference with the exception register. On Linux-based NFS/Samba servers, check xinetd/inetd configuration, vsftpd or proftpd configuration, and Samba's smb.conf for any enabled legacy services.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If any of these protocols appear enabled (e.g., 'disable = no' in xinetd entries, uncommented service definitions), a corresponding approved exception must exist in the security register for this attribute to be true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all listening network services on the storage server to identify whether FTP (21), telnet (23), rsh (514), or HTTP management (80/8080) ports are active, confirming what protocols are actually exposed and therefore require justification.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any line showing LISTEN state on ports 21, 23, 80, 514, 8080 indicates an insecure protocol is active; if no such lines appear, the protocols are not enabled and justification is moot (attribute can remain false safely).

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a network scanner or assessment workstation, perform a targeted port scan against the storage server to independently verify which legacy protocol ports are externally reachable, then match findings against the exception register to determine whether documented justification exists.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ports reported as 'open' with identified service banners (e.g., vsftpd, telnetd, rshd, Apache httpd) confirm active protocols; each open legacy protocol port must have a corresponding approved exception for this attribute to be set to true.

typical_values: false — most hardened storage deployments disable all legacy protocols entirely, making justification unnecessary; this is the secure default and most commonly observed value in compliant environments

true — occasionally observed in environments with legacy backup agents requiring FTP, older NAS management interfaces exposing HTTP, or mainframe integration requiring rsh, provided a formal exception with compensating controls (VLAN isolation, IDS monitoring, protocol proxies) has been approved and documented
